reference.source: Williams Hematology / Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
clinicalPearls: A group of inherited anaemias defined by ring sideroblasts in the marrow, reflecting iron-laden mitochondria encircling the erythroblast nucleus
The commonest form is X-linked, caused by ALAS2 mutations affecting the first enzyme of haem synthesis, and characteristically responds to pyridoxine
Autosomal recessive SLC25A38 disease is the next most frequent and tends to be more severe and pyridoxine-unresponsive
Syndromic variants exist, including mitochondrial DNA deletion in Pearson syndrome and SLC19A2-related thiamine-responsive anaemia with diabetes and deafness
The blood film typically shows a dimorphic or hypochromic microcytic anaemia, though the mean cell volume can be normal or raised in some forms
Systemic iron overload develops even without transfusion because ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin and enhances iron absorption
Diagnosis combines iron-stained marrow showing ring sideroblasts with targeted gene panels; a pyridoxine trial is warranted where ALAS2 disease is suspected
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital sideroblastic anaemias result from defects that impair mitochondrial haem biosynthesis, iron-sulphur cluster assembly, or mitochondrial protein handling within developing erythroblasts. When haem synthesis stalls, iron that has been imported into the mitochondrion cannot be incorporated into protoporphyrin and instead accumulates as insoluble deposits in perinuclear mitochondria, producing the pathognomonic ring sideroblast. ALAS2 mutations cripple delta-aminolaevulinate synthase, the pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent first committed step of the pathway; SLC25A38 disrupts the mitochondrial glycine transporter that supplies substrate. The failure of effective haemoglobinisation causes ineffective erythropoiesis, and the accompanying suppression of hepcidin drives excess dietary iron absorption and progressive parenchymal iron loading.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired clonal sideroblastic anaemia (myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts)
Iron deficiency and other microcytic anaemias
Copper deficiency or zinc excess causing sideroblastic change
Alcohol- or drug-induced (for example isoniazid) reversible sideroblastic anaemia
additionalInvestigations: Bone marrow aspirate with Perls (Prussian blue) iron stain to demonstrate ring sideroblasts
Full blood count and blood film assessing red cell indices and dimorphism
Iron studies including ferritin and transferrin saturation to gauge overload
Targeted next-generation sequencing panel (ALAS2, SLC25A38, and syndromic genes)
A supervised pyridoxine trial where ALAS2 disease is likely
Screening for syndromic features such as diabetes, deafness, or exocrine pancreatic dysfunction
redFlags: Evidence of iron overload with cardiac, hepatic, or endocrine dysfunction despite few or no transfusions
Severe transfusion-dependent anaemia presenting in infancy
Syndromic features suggesting mitochondrial disease such as lactic acidosis or multiorgan failure
Progressive cytopenias raising concern for clonal or marrow-failure evolution
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on subtype: pyridoxine-responsive ALAS2 disease can be well controlled, whereas SLC25A38 and syndromic forms are more severe, and long-term morbidity is dominated by iron overload requiring vigilant monitoring and chelation.
pitfalls: Assuming a microcytic anaemia is iron deficiency and giving iron, which worsens overload
Missing the pyridoxine-responsive ALAS2 phenotype and failing to trial the vitamin
Confusing congenital disease with acquired myelodysplasia, which requires different management
Neglecting iron chelation because the patient is not transfusion dependent
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
